title: LTCG Tax Tweaks: What Budget 2027-28 Might Bring
description: The government is reportedly considering adjustments to the Long-Term Capital Gains (LTCG) tax framework as Budget 2027-28 approaches. This evaluation include.

faq.q: What is Long-Term Capital Gains (LTCG) tax?
faq.a: LTCG tax is levied on profits earned from selling capital assets (like shares, property, mutual funds) after holding them for a specified long-term period, which varies by asset type. The tax rates and exemptions also differ.

faq.q: What is the current LTCG tax rate for equity investments?
faq.a: For listed equity shares and equity-oriented mutual funds, LTCG exceeding ₹1 lakh in a financial year are taxed at 10% without indexation, provided the asset was held for more than 12 months.

faq.q: What is indexation benefit in capital gains tax?
faq.a: Indexation allows you to adjust the cost of acquisition of an asset for inflation using the Cost Inflation Index (CII) published by the Income Tax Department. This reduces the taxable capital gain, lowering your tax liability. It's currently available for assets like real estate and debt mutual funds.

faq.q: Will the proposed LTCG tax changes be retrospective?
faq.a: Tax changes are generally prospective, meaning they apply from a future date. While retrospective amendments are possible in specific cases, they are less common for broad tax structure changes like LTCG. Official announcements will clarify the effective date.

faq.q: How might LTCG changes affect Non-Resident Indians (NRIs)?
faq.a: Any changes to LTCG rules will apply to NRIs investing in Indian assets. NRIs should particularly assess the impact on their net returns, tax filings in India, and how these changes interact with Double Taxation Avoidance Agreements (DTAAs) with their country of residence.

faq.q: Where can I find the official rules for capital gains tax in India?
faq.a: The official rules and regulations regarding capital gains tax are available on the Income Tax Department's website under the Income Tax Act, 1961. You can refer to relevant sections like 112A, 112, 54, 54F, etc.
